entries.title: NITROUS.IO 101 - Teach Coding
entries.body: NITROUS.IO 101 - Teach Coding Last Updated on: 30 January 2015 This is a quick tutorial that shows you how you can use Nitrous.IO for the purposes of conducting coding lessons. Check out our blog post to find out what makes Nitrous.IO the ideal platform for coding lessons. You’d need a Nitrous account to execute these steps, sign up for free and get provisioned with a free development box. CREATE A BOX Development Boxes or “boxes” are the heart and soul of the Nitrous experience. Basic, free boxes come with stock setups: Rails, Python, Node.js, Go, PHP & Meteor. We include most everything else you need to start teaching, like imagemagick and more. To create a new free box, just click the “New Box” button on your dashboard after signing in. 1. Pick a box template Select which default stock development environments you prefer to start coding on. We support the following setups. Shoot us an email if you want us to support a different stack. 2. Enter a unique name Pick a descriptive box name, the best practice here is to describe the stack or the project (if you’re only going to keep one project on each box, that’s up to you). 3. Pick a region We will default the region to whichever is closest to your current IP address, though if you’re travelling and want the box closer to your hometown, then just pick the region closest to you. Provisioning Once you’ve clicked “Create Box”, you’ll need to wait a few seconds while we provision the box. This is typically pretty speedy, but might take up to a minute. After the box is provisioned, you’ll be kicked into the box information page. Simply click the “IDE” button and you’re ready to start your coding lesson! TEACH You can create as many projects as you would like within a single Nitrous box. The only limitation to this is the amount of storage space you use, which not only counts the project files but also modules, different versions of Ruby installed, etc. Below you will see a screenshot of how you could setup your directories within Nitrous.IO. All projects should be placed within the ~/workspace folder, and configuration files can be placed in your home directory ~/. Build your app just as you normally would on your local environment. If you find that you need to install additional packages/tools, you can easily get what you need using our Autoparts Package Manager. COLLAB MODE You can nudge on your students’ learning progress by having them add you as a Collaborator to their boxes. To do so, select Collaborate → Manage Collaborators from the dropdown menu. Type your email address in the following field. You’ll receive an email invite and your students’ boxes will appear in your list of boxes thereafter: Now you can access any box to make necessary repairs/code-edits to aid your students’ learning. Simply pick the file you want to make changes to and select Collab Mode - your students will be able to see your changes live in realtime. PREVIEW APP At the end of the lesson, students can preview and share their newly created web app on a public URL while it is running within their active session. The Preview menu in the Web IDE displays links to some common default ports, which you can click to open a new window in your browser. Ports 1024 - 10,000 are open for HTTP, and port 80 is forwarded to port 3000. If your app is running on port 80 in the terminal, navigate to ‘Preview > Port 3000’ in the menu. If the app is running on another port not found in the menu then you will need to change this within the address bar (e.g. http://ruby-21200.usw1-2.nitrousbox.com:8080). With a public URL, students would have something to take home with from the lesson and share their learnings with friends and families. If they want to carry on learning independently, they can easily log back into their box while at home and continue from where they left off. TWEET SHARE SHARE SHARE

entries.title: Pair Programming
entries.body: Pair Programming Last Updated on: 06 February 2015 Here’s a quick tutorial that brings you up to speed with Pair Programming on Nitrous.IO’s collaborative editor. Sign up for a free account to unlock the benefits of cloud collaboration in real-time, if you don’t already have one. Check out our featured blog post for a brief introduction to this effective Agile Development practice, that has been used by companies like Pivotal Labs. Start the Web IDE Create a box on Nitrous.IO, or you can use a box that you’ve already created. Pair programming works on any box template. In your list of boxes, click the IDE button to boot up the IDE for your box: Adding Collaborators Now we’ve got to give access to our friends / colleagues so they can access our box. Note that with adding collaborators comes great responsibility. Notably, you must trust who you are adding to your box. For extra security, you should practice the following: Use SSH Key with passphrase If you’ve already added an SSH Key to Nitrous.IO without a passphrase, you’ll need to delete it and re-generate one with a passphrase. Using HTTPS authentication with Github should prompt you for your password, thus restricting any abuse from collaborators (but they’re your friends, why would they do that?!). Better safe then sorry…my friends have done some evil things to my desktop background…and my forehead with a very, very permanent marker. Okay, back to business. In the IDE, Click the “Collaborate” menu item in the top navigation, and select “Manage Collaborators”: A list of any collaborators you’ve already added will appear. Enter the Nitrous.IO username, or email of the person you’d like to add to your box. Nitrous Users & New Users If you’re inviting a user with their username, they’ll receive an email and the box will appear in their list of boxes: If they don’t have an account yet, they’ll receive an invite to Nitrous, and will be able to access only boxes to which they’ve been added as a collaborator. Collaborating on Files Ok, now lets get to the good part. Once you and your pair programming buddy have opened the IDE, you can edit files simultaneously. First, and most importantly, you’ll need to open the same file. Luckily, we put file status notifications in the chat window on the right of the IDE. Chat To open the chat, just click the little “message” icon on the right of the IDE. This will toggle the chat window which has a few valuable features. You can check who else is online by hovering over the group icon. Alternatively, you could just write a message in the chat saying “what’s up”, but sometimes people are around and are just ignoring you because you’re not the most “likable guy”…bleh whatever, screw ‘em. File status Assuming someone has joined the room and opened a file, you’ll see a file status message in the chat window. This is a great shortcut to open the same file to start editing. Collaborate! Now that we have the same file open, we can collaborate. You’ll need to turn “Collab Mode” on for each file. To turn on Collab Mode, just click the little button on the top-right of the file: Now, when you edit, your friend will see the changes happening live in their browser. They can type at the same time and it will show up in your browser. Tmux Session If you’re running a server or long-running process that you don’t want to interrupt when you mistakenly close your browser window, create a tmux session by typing the following command in the IDE console window: tmux new -s my_session Once you’ve done that, your work will be constantly stored in a persistent session to which you and your friend can always reconnect to. You can also see what each other type in the console window in real-time. Attach back to the session you’ve created if you happen to mistakenly exit your browser window : tmux attach -t my_session Now you can reap the benefits of pair programming no matter where you are, without being physically confined to a single workstation shared with your programming partner. You will unlock the benefits of cloud collaboration using Nitrous IO - sign up for a free account. Check out our featured blog post for a brief introduction to this effective Agile Development practice, that has been used by companies like Pivotal Labs. TWEET SHARE SHARE SHARE

entries.title: Install Magento on Nitrous
entries.body: Install Magento on Nitrous Last Updated on: 23 February 2015 This installation guide was contributed by Matt Rhys-Davies - Ecommerce Analyst. The following guide will detail how to install Magento, the hugely popular open source ecommerce framework on Nitrous. We’ll walk through setting up your box on Nitrous, grabbing a copy of Magento and getting it setup. Prerequisites A Nitrous account Create a PHP Box Now that you’re in your account the first step is to create your environment. This is be done by selecting “Boxes” from the top navigation, and then clicking “New Box” on the following screen, which will take you to a page where you specify the name and language for the box. Magento runs in PHP so we’ll need to select PHP and give the box a name - I’ve simply gone for “magento-box”. Your screen should now look like the below screenshot. Now click “Create Box” and after a short delay you’ll be taken to your IDE, already provisioned with Apache & MySQL. Create a MySQL Database Whilst you can manage the MySQL database from the command line if you are so inclined, I am more comfortable with phpMyAdmin, so let’s get that installed. From the top navigation, click Autoparts > Manage Packages. Search for “phpMyAdmin” and click the install button once located. We now need to specify a password for the root database user as phpMyAdmin will not allow access without a password. In the terminal window that you’ll find near at the bottom of the IDE, type the following: $ mysqladmin -u root password YOUR_PASSWORD This sets the password for the root user as “YOUR_PASSWORD”. Within the menu bar, navigate to Preview > Port 3000 to open your site within a new tab. From that page click the phpmyadmin/ subdirectory and then login with the username: “root” and the password that was just set. Now you’re in phpMyAdmin, click the Databases tab at the top and in the following screen enter a name for your database in the “Create database” field (ex. “magento”) and hit the “Create” button. Now that we’ve created our database, let’s go back to the IDE so we can acquire the Magento files. Install Magento In the terminal window at the bottom of the IDE, cd into the webroot and download Magento: $ cd ~/workspace/www && wget http://www.magentocommerce.com/downloads/assets/1.9.1.0/magento-1.9.1.0.tar.gz Note: 1.9.1.0 refers to the current release of Magento Community at the time of writing. This may have changed since, refer to http://www.magentocommerce.com/download in order to find the latest version ID. We now need to extract the files from the tar, so you will need to execute the following: $ tar -zxvf magento-1.9.1.0.tar.gz When we unzipped the tar file in the command above, all the files were unpacked into a magento/ directory. Let’s move all the application’s files and directories into the web root. To do this, enter the following. $ mv magento/* magento/.htaccess . Now we need to specify permissions on our media, var and app/etc directories respectively with the below commands. $ chmod -R o+w media var && chmod o+w app/etc Finally, let’s remove the tar file with the following command: $ rm -rf magento/ magento-1.9.1.0.tar.gz If all has gone to plan, by hitting the refresh button at the top of the file tree you will see the following. Now we are required to run through the Magento install UI which will create the necessary files and database tables for the application. Within the menu bar navigate to Preview > Port 3000 which will open a new tab. The last time when we did this we were presented a blank page with a single link to phpMyAdmin. Now you will be greeted with Magento’s installation wizard. Click to agree to the terms and conditions. Assuming you do agree to them. If you don’t, well I guess you’re a little stuck. On the following page specify your Locale, Time Zone and the Default Currency, and then click continue. On the next page you will be prompted to configure the database connection. Host: This should be left as localhost - this is how Nitrous will enable connection to the database Database Name: This should be what you named the database when it was created in the above step, mine is “magento” Username: This should be left as root User Password: This is whatever you specified previously when we set the root password using mysqladmin Tables Prefix: This should be left blank Leave the Base URL & Admin Path as they are, and select the checkbox to enable Apache Rewrites. Leave session storage to be stored in the file system. Now hit continue. It will take about a minute or two for Magento to create the database, and then it will forward you onto the final configuration page (screenshot below) where you will need to specify the name, user name, password, and email address of the admin user. Note: During the setup process you may experience the page timing out. If this is the case then you may want to increase the box’s memory up to 1024 MB to resolve the issue. This is only needed during the installation and can be reduced later, once Magento’s successfully installed. Hitting continue on this page will complete the installation of Magento. The final page is where your encryption key will be published; make sure you save a copy of it as you may need it in the future. There’s also a short survey to fill in, which I consider worthwhile in order to provide some insight to the Magento team. We’re done. We now have a fully functioning Magento instance with what was hopefully a short and pain-free installation. Welcome to Magento; the most powerful open source ecommerce framework around. entries.title: Getting Started with WordPress
entries.body: Getting Started with WordPress Last Updated on: 27 February 2015 WordPress is web software you can use to create a website or blog. It is a CMS (content management system), meaning you can edit and maintain the content within a central interface. Prerequisites A Nitrous.IO Account Create a Box First you will need to create a box that we’ll install WordPress on. Select PHP as your environment and give the box a name (ex. WordPress). Select continue and wait while Nitrous builds your dev environment. Install WordPress To install WordPress within your box you will need to use the package manager, Autoparts. Navigate in the Menu to Autoparts > Install Parts…, and search for WordPress. Installing WordPress will automatically install all dependencies if not yet installed (PHP5, Apache2, MySQL). Once installed, the WordPress installation can be found in ~/workspace/www/WordPress. Configuration To connect to your new site, navigate in the menu bar to Preview > Port 3000. Once a new tab opens up you should see the Wordpress/ directory leading to your new site. Click on that directory and select your language. On the next page you will be prompted configure your new site. The fields you need to fill in here are: Site Title: This is what will be displayed in the top of browsers so do ensure it is descriptive of your site content. User Name: This is the user name that you will use to login to the admin panel Password: This is your password to access the admin panel, so make sure it’s strong and secure. Email Address: The address that is specified here is the email address used for the administration of the site. Privacy: As this is a development box I would suggest to uncheck the Privacy field otherwise search engines may start to index your content, which has the potential to cause slight issues further down the line. Just be sure that when you port the system to production that you change the setting to be indexed: Admin > Settings > Reading > Search Engine Visibility. Once you’ve filled out these fields, select Install WordPress. You have successfully installed WordPress on Nitrous, and are able to login to the admin panel and start developing. Updates to this guide were contributed by Matt Rhys-Davies - WordPress Ecommerce Developer and Analyst. TWEET SHARE SHARE SHARE

entries.body: Coding Interview Last Updated on: 04 March 2015 Here’s an in-depth tutorial on how you can conduct live Coding Interviews using Nitrous.IO in Collab Mode and tmux. If you are new to Nitrous.IO, simply sign up for a free account, create a development box in seconds and you’d be all set for this tutorial. Do check out our blog post to find out what makes Nitrous.IO a great platform for coding interviews. Start the Web IDE Create a box on Nitrous, or you can use a box that you’ve already created. You can use any box template to conduct interviews. In your list of boxes, click the IDE button to boot up the IDE for your box: Adding Collaborators (Candidates) Now we’ve got to give access to our candidates so they can access our box. In the IDE, Click the “Collaborate” menu item in the top navigation, and select “Manage Collaborators”: A modal with a list of collaborators you’ve already added will appear. Enter the Nitrous.IO username, or email of the candidate you’d like to add to your box. Nitrous Users & New Users If you’re inviting a Nitrous User with their username, they’ll receive an email and the box will appear in their list of boxes: If they don’t have an account yet, they’ll receive an invite to Nitrous, and will be able to access only boxes to which they’ve been added as a collaborator. Collaborating on Files On to the good part. Once you and the candidate have opened the IDE, you can edit files simultaneously. First, and most importantly, you’ll need to open the same file. Luckily, we put file status notifications in the chat window on the right of the IDE. File status Assuming the candidate has joined the room and opened a file, you’ll see a file status message in the chat window. This is a great shortcut to open the same file to start the interview. Chat (in case of Remote Coding Interview) To open the chat, just click the little “message” icon on the right of the IDE. This will toggle the chat window which has a few valuable features. You can check who else is online by hovering over the group icon. Start the Interview! Now that we have the same file open, we can begin the interview. You’ll need to turn “Collab Mode” on for each file. To turn on Collab Mode, just click the little button on the top-right of the file. Tell the candidate to do the same. Now, when the candidate edits, you will see the changes happening live in your browser. You can type at the same time and it will show up in their browser. Tmux Session If you require your candidate to run a server or long-running process that neither of you want to interrupt by mistakenly closing the browser window, simply use tmux (a terminal multiplexer). Create a tmux session by typing the following command in the IDE console window: tmux new -s my_session Once you’ve done that, your terminal session will be accessible to your candidate. You can also see what each other types in the console window in real-time. Tell your candidate to attach to the session you’ve created by running the below: tmux attach -t my_session You can return to the session if you close your browser window by running the same command. Note: Remember to remove the candidate’s box access via ‘Collaborate’ => ‘Manage Collaborators’ once the interview has included. TWEET SHARE SHARE SHARE
